## 1 Abstract

**mhpfilter** splits a macroeconomic time series into a trend and a
cycle. This vignette takes the quarterly real GDP of the United States
from the raw series to the three filters of the package, their
comparison, many series at once and a plain-language reading of the
results. The later vignettes give the theory (vignette 2), the two
papers behind the package (vignettes 3 and 4), the simulation study
(vignette 5), the application (vignette 6) and the checks of the code
(vignette 7).

## 2 The data

`us_macro` holds quarterly real GDP, consumption and investment of the
United States from 1959 to 2009 (FRED). As a `ts` the series keeps its
dates, and every result of the package keeps them too.

``` r

data(us_macro)
head(us_macro)
```

      year quarter      gdp consumption investment
    1 1959       1 2710.349      1707.4    286.898
    2 1959       2 2778.801      1733.7    310.859
    3 1959       3 2775.488      1751.8    289.226
    4 1959       4 2785.204      1753.7    299.356
    5 1960       1 2847.699      1770.5    331.722
    6 1960       2 2834.390      1792.9    298.152

``` r

gdp <- ts(data = us_macro$gdp, start = c(1959, 1), frequency = 4)
```

## 3 Three filters

### 3.1 The HP filter

The filter of Hodrick and Prescott (1997) fits a smooth trend \\\vg\\ to
the series \\\vx\\ by minimising \\ \sum\_{t=1}^{T}(x_t - g_t)^2 +
\lambda\sum\_{t=2}^{T-1}\left\[(g\_{t+1} - g_t) - (g_t -
g\_{t-1})\right\]^2 , \\ and the cycle is \\\vc = \vx - \vg\\. The
smoothing parameter \\\lambda\\ is conventionally 1600 for quarterly
data. On the logarithm of a series the cycle is close to the percentage
deviation from the trend.

``` r

hp <-
  hp_filter(
      x         = log(gdp)
    , lambda    = 1600
    , as_dt     = TRUE
    , log_scale = FALSE
    )
hp
```

With `as_dt = TRUE`, the default kept from version 0.1.0, the result is
a `data.table`; `as_dt = FALSE` gives a list with methods for printing
and plotting.

### 3.2 The modified HP filter

The modified HP filter of McDermott (1997), assessed by Choudhary, Hanif
and Iqbal (2014), lets the data choose \\\lambda\\: it tries every
\\\lambda = 1, 2, \dots\\ and keeps the one that minimises a generalised
cross-validation criterion.

``` r

mhp <-
  mhp_filter(
      x          = log(gdp)
    , max_lambda = 100000
    , as_dt      = FALSE
    , log_scale  = FALSE
    , criterion  = "approximate"
    )
mhp
```

    Modified HP Filter Result
    ==============================
    Observations: 203
    Optimal lambda: 683
    GCV: 2.82e-04

    Cycle Statistics:
      Mean: -1.634e-13
      SD:   0.01333
      AR1:  0.828
      Range: 0.07802

    Sources: Hodrick and Prescott (1997); McDermott (1997); Coe and McDermott
    (1997); Choudhary et al. (2014); Choudhary et al. (2014, MATLAB code). Full
    references: mhp_cite(x).

``` r

plot(x = mhp)
```

![](data:image/webp;base64,)

``` r

plot(x = mhp, which = "gcv")
```

![](data:image/webp;base64,)

### 3.3 The fully modified HP filter

The HP filter has too little information at the ends of a series, so its
trend follows the last observations too closely and the end of the cycle
is biased towards zero, just where a policy maker needs it most. The
fully modified HP filter of Hanif, Iqbal and Choudhary (2017) raises
\\\lambda\\ at the first and last observations, with weights chosen to
make the filter at the ends behave like the filter in the middle, and
chooses \\\lambda\\ from the data as the modified HP filter does. The
published code filters the logarithm of the series and returns the trend
and the cycle in levels; `log_scale = TRUE` does the same.

``` r

fm <-
  fmhp_filter(
      x               = gdp
    , max_lambda      = 3000
    , k_linear        = 15
    , k_quadratic     = NULL
    , alpha_linear    = seq(from = 0, to = 2000, by = 10)
    , alpha_quadratic = seq(from = 0, to = 2000, by = 5)
    , schemes         = c("linear", "quadratic")
    , form            = "rows"
    , lambda          = NULL
    , log_scale       = TRUE
    , as_dt           = FALSE
    )
fm
```

    Fully modified HP Filter Result
    ==============================
    Observations: 203
    Fully modified lambda: 1448  (modified HP lambda: 683 )
    End-point weights: quadratic, alpha = 15 on 22 end values; loss = 0.6163
    GCV: 3.336e-04
    Filtered on the log scale; cycle = series - trend in levels

    Cycle Statistics:
      Mean: -2.603
      SD:   120.4
      AR1:  0.9522
      Range: 900

    Sources: Hanif et al. (2017); Hanif (2017); Bloechl (2014); McDermott (1997);
    Hodrick and Prescott (1997). Full references: mhp_cite(x).

``` r

fm$schemes
```

          scheme     k alpha      loss lambda          gcv
          <char> <int> <num>     <num>  <int>        <num>
    1:    linear    15   240 0.8548936   1169 0.0003168500
    2: quadratic    22    15 0.6163442   1448 0.0003335623

``` r

plot(x = fm, which = "lambda")
```

![](data:image/webp;base64,)

The smoothing parameter rises from 1448 in the middle to 8708 at the
first and last observation (quadratic weights on 22 values at each end).

## 4 Comparing the filters

[`fmhp_compare()`](https://myaseen208.com/mhpfilter/reference/fmhp_compare.md)
filters the series with the three filters and compares the cycles and
their end-point loss, the measure of end-point bias used by Hanif et
al. (2017): zero for a filter that treats the ends like the middle.

``` r

cmp <-
  fmhp_compare(
      x          = gdp
    , frequency  = "quarterly"
    , max_lambda = 3000
    , log_scale  = TRUE
    , end_share  = 0.1
    )
cmp
```

                  method lambda   cycle_sd    cycle_mean       ar1 cycle_range
                  <char>  <num>      <num>         <num>     <num>       <num>
    1:                HP   1600 0.01543904  4.942713e-12 0.8668207  0.08590516
    2:       Modified HP    683 0.01333176 -1.634336e-13 0.8280266  0.07801575
    3: Fully modified HP   1448 0.01618038 -4.145448e-05 0.8815215  0.08713978
                gcv      loss    sd_ends  sd_middle
              <num>     <num>      <num>      <num>
    1:           NA 1.7617778 0.01458541 0.01568213
    2: 0.0002819926 1.7652928 0.01202396 0.01366805
    3: 0.0003335623 0.7898641 0.01930994 0.01538061

The fully modified HP filter cuts the loss of the HP filter by more than
half. Its cycle is also more variable at the ends than in the middle,
unlike the cycles of the other two filters: the end-point bias of the HP
filter shows as cycles that are too small at the ends.

``` r

plot_comparison(
    x          = log(gdp)
  , frequency  = "quarterly"
  , max_lambda = 100000
  , show_cycle = TRUE
  , fmhp       = TRUE
  )
```

![](data:image/webp;base64,)

## 5 Many series

[`mhp_batch()`](https://myaseen208.com/mhpfilter/reference/mhp_batch.md)
and
[`fmhp_batch()`](https://myaseen208.com/mhpfilter/reference/fmhp_batch.md)
filter every column of a matrix; series of different lengths can share
it, padded with missing values at the start or the end.

``` r

X <- as.matrix(us_macro[, c("gdp", "consumption", "investment")])
fb <-
  fmhp_batch(
      X               = X
    , max_lambda      = 3000
    , k_linear        = 15
    , k_quadratic     = NULL
    , alpha_linear    = seq(from = 0, to = 2000, by = 10)
    , alpha_quadratic = seq(from = 0, to = 2000, by = 5)
    , schemes         = c("linear", "quadratic")
    , form            = "rows"
    , lambda          = NULL
    , log_scale       = TRUE
    )
attr(x = fb, which = "lambdas")
```

            series lambda          gcv lambda_mhp    scheme alpha     k      loss
            <char>  <int>        <num>      <int>    <char> <num> <int>     <num>
    1:         gdp   1448 0.0003335623        683 quadratic    15    22 0.6163442
    2: consumption   1261 0.0002248243        534 quadratic    15    22 0.5850792
    3:  investment   2961 0.0073465762       1009 quadratic    20    22 0.6728679

``` r

plot_batch(
    x         = fb
  , show      = "cycle"
  , facet     = TRUE
  , highlight = NULL
  )
```

![](data:image/webp;base64,)

## 6 Reading the results

[`mhp_interpret()`](https://myaseen208.com/mhpfilter/reference/mhp_interpret.md)
reads a result in plain language, from its numbers, and ends with the
sources of the method.

``` r

mhp_interpret(
    x   = fm
  , top = 3
  )
```

    Fully modified HP filter

    The fully modified HP filter chose lambda = 1,448 (the modified HP filter
    alone: 683) and quadratic end-point weights on 22 values at each end, which
    cut the end-point loss of the HP filter with the same lambda by 65%.

    Findings:
    - Cycle (log scale, about the share of the trend): standard deviation 0.0162,
      first-order autocorrelation 0.88, range 0.0871.
    - Largest positive cycle values (booms) at 2000Q2, 1978Q4, 1999Q4; largest
      negative ones (recessions) at 2009Q2, 2009Q3, 2009Q1.
    - Linear weights: loss 0.855 (alpha = 240); quadratic weights: loss 0.616
      (alpha = 15); the quadratic scheme was kept.

    Recommendations:
    - Compare the filters on this series with fmhp_compare() (moments of the
      cycles and end-point loss).

    Cautions:
    - The last values of the cycle are revised as new observations arrive: read
      them with care.

    Sources:
    - Hanif, M. N., Iqbal, J. and Choudhary, M. A. (2017). Fully modified HP
      filter. SBP Working Paper Series, No. 88, State Bank of Pakistan.
    - Hanif, M. N. (2017). Fully modified HP filter function (MATLAB code).
      MATLAB Central File Exchange, 63198.
    - Bloechl, A. (2014). Reducing the excess variability of the Hodrick-Prescott
      filter by flexible penalization. Discussion Paper 2014-1, University of
      Munich.
    - McDermott, C. J. (1997). An automatic method for choosing the smoothing
      parameter in the HP filter. Unpublished, International Monetary Fund,
      Washington DC.
    - Hodrick, R. J. and Prescott, E. C. (1997). Postwar U.S. business cycles: an
      empirical investigation. Journal of Money, Credit and Banking, 29(1), 1-16.
      doi:10.2307/2953682
